Dudes Online Are So Mad That ‘Grand Theft Auto 6’ Makes Them Respect Women

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (889 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Grand Theft Auto games never actually taught someone how to knock over a bank or survive a shootout with police, but the latest storyline in the franchise serves up some valuable lessons about what it means to be in a loving and committed relationship.
  • This isn’t sitting well with a histrionic minority of right-wing gamers who have been warning for months that GTA VI would be intolerably “woke.” While their attempt at a manufactured backlash is going even more poorly than the one that greeted Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey this summer (the day of its official release, the game is already closing in on 20 million copies sold and $2 billion in revenue), these streamers and commentators are throwing tantrums about gender politics anyway.
  • “RIP GTA,” one X user somberly concluded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Grand Theft Auto games never actually taught someone how to knock over a bank or survive a shootout with police, but the latest storyline in the franchise serves up some valuable lessons about what it means to be in a loving and committed relationship.

This isn’t sitting well with a histrionic minority of right-wing gamers who have been warning for months that GTA VI would be intolerably “woke.” While their attempt at a manufactured backlash is going even more poorly than the one that greeted Christopher Nolan’s film The Odyssey this summer (the day of its official release, the game is already closing in on 20 million copies sold and $2 billion in revenue), these streamers and commentators are throwing tantrums about gender politics anyway.

“RIP GTA,” one X user somberly concluded. “Killed by women.”.

In case you’re among the handful of skeptics who didn’t launch their single-player campaign in GTA VI at midnight last night after 13 years of desperate anticipation: This latest installment in the satirical crime-caper series is led by dual protagonists, Jason and Lucia, a couple whose meet-cute involves them both trying to jack the same car. Living together in a fictionalized version of South Florida, they look to get by on the wrong side of the law—but the player must also negotiate their emotional bond through domestic chores and acts of affection.

“This game is such woke slop,” wrote one blue-check user on X who has posted almost nothing besides negative reactions to the game for the past week. The post included a screenshot of a fully optional GTA VI mission that describes how the Lucia character will appreciate a flower delivery and indicates with a heart icon that the action will strengthen feelings between her and Jason.

Other choices you can make as Jason to get closer to Lucia (sex is very much on the table) include picking up groceries, getting a haircut or beard trim, gifting her a piece of jewelry, and repainting walls in the house.

Sources indicate that the concept of role-playing as a nice and non-performatively masculine boyfriend has come as a rude shock to those more interested in explosions and mayhem. The right-wing streamer Zack Hoyt, known online as Asmongold, was dumbfounded to find himself unclogging a sink in a scene where Jason is trying to collect back rent from a tenant who refuses the money until the plumbing is fixed. “I actually have to fucking fix this bitch’s sink?” Hoyt asked on stream. “Why can’t she do this?” Elsewhere, when running errands for Lucia as Jason, Hoyt referred to GTA VI as a “cuck simulator.” (That Hoyt thinks caring for a romantic partner makes someone a cuckold is perhaps an unfortunate glimpse into his dating history.).

More frustrated responses to the massively popular GTA VI came from looksmaxxing influencer Braden Peters, aka Clavicular, (the game required too much “simping for girls,” the streamer, presently facing multiple rape charges, complained on X), anti-woke gamer activist Mark Kern, aka Grummz (he called the housework “mundane crap”), and misinformation superspreader Dom Lucre, who falsely claimed that Rockstar had specifically made it impossible to open fire in a gay nightclub. (Washington Post critic Gene Park pointed out that the club in question was not LGBTQ-specific and that the mechanics of the game don’t allow you to shoot anyone in any kind of club.) These comments came alongside the predictable gripes over supposedly “overweight” female characters with insufficiently large breasts.

If the Tates, incels, and other far-right reactionaries of the world are so bent out of shape, it’s probably because whereas GTA once punched down at marginalized groups like sex workers and transgender people, bigots and self-styled alpha males are now the butt of the joke. The Vice City of GTA VI is bristling with parodies of toxic manosphere content and crypto scams. Random characters on the street will spout MAGA-coded conspiracy theories and call you a “libtard” or “commie socialist” if you walk into them. These touches seem to have made the game into “a bug zapper for chuds,” as one Bluesky user put it. (That hasn’t stopped Republicans and Trump allies from trying and failing to score political points with the game.).

Yet the provocation of asking guys to consider acts of service for a virtual girlfriend could prove the most revolutionary element of GTA VI.

Sources indicate that it’s not that games like The Sims haven’t explored this territory before, and Rockstar’s own Red Dead Redemption franchise paid similar attention to quotidian detail. In those frontier-set narratives, your cowboy character had to make coffee over campfires and even clean up manure in barns. By addressing characters’ most basic needs—you can even manage personal hygiene by showering—GTA VI recalls some of the slower and quieter aspects of that franchise.

In a recent development, what’s truly remarkable, though, is that adult men who grew up indulging their most selfish and sociopathic instincts in the older GTA games have had their nostalgia for those escapades cleverly complicated with real-life problems. They can still steal cars, sell drugs, and rise through the ranks of a seedy underworld. That will always be the appeal of the series, which is now asking eternally aggrieved culture warriors to consider a vital question: What if you didn’t have to do it alone?

#47819. What has changed in James Bond films over the decades

📅 05 Oct 2022 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1173 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Dw ↗ Open Full Page

What has changed in James Bond films over the decades

📅 05 Oct 2022 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1173 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios declared on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.
  • This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.
  • The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival.".
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

After years of speculation, Amazon MGM Studios declared on Monday that Robert Pattinson would be taking on the role of James Bond following Daniel Craig's departure after five hit films in the spy series.

This year alone, Pattinson has starred in "The Odyssey," "The Drama" and "Primetime." He is also famous for his role as "Twilight" vampire Edward Cullen.

The upcoming Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, an Oscar nominee known for movies such as the "Dune" trilogy and "Arrival.".

Industry observers note that based on the spy novels by author Ian Fleming, the Bond franchise — about a British secret agent known for his charm and ⁠a ⁠fondness for martinis "shaken, not stirred" — is among the longest-running and highest-grossing in Hollywood history. ​​​​​​​.

The first film in the series, "Dr. No," premiered in London on October 5, 1962.

Playing the leading role, Agent 007, was an unknown actor: Sean Connery.

In the film, we are first introduced to his character as he sits in a casino across from an attractive woman who is about to gamble away her fortune. When she asks 007 his name, the camera pans to Bond lighting a cigarette. With a smoldering look in his eye, he utters the legendary words: "Bond, James Bond.".

Recent findings suggest that shortly thereafter in the film, 007 receives an assignment to fly to Jamaica and investigate the murder of another M16 agent. He eventually tracks down a Chinese-German criminal scientist who is bent on destroying the US space program and achieving world domination.

Industry observers note that in principle, this story is the basis of all of 25 James Bond films. Whether the villain is Dr. No, Blofeld, Goldfinger or Le Chiffre, they all aim for one thing: world domination. But to do so, they have to get past James Bond whose gunfire and wild chase scenes inevitably spoil their plans.

It has been revealed that although many fan forums consider "Dr. No" to be one of the best Bond films, the movie would never be made in the same way today.

Firstly, one could write entire books about the omnipresent sexism and machismo that the character James Bond has displayed over the decades.

Certainly there would have to be a thick chapter dedicated to the women in his films, who are typically portrayed as naive, willingly flinging themselves into Bond's arms, seeking protection. Sometimes they are sophisticated female antagonists who lose control at the thought of hopping into bed with the secret agent.

It has been revealed that whether friend of foe, each film had at least one Bond girl — and often more: More than 60 love interests have appeared in the films. Their names, like "Honey" or "Pussy Galore" would never be acceptable today. In more recent decades, female roles in Bond films have changed — as has Bond himself.

In the last five films in which Daniel Craig has played Bond, he is seen as a man who is tough on the outside and soft on the inside — and who is not always lucky with women.

Aside from the portrayal of women on screen, there are also plenty of other details in "Dr. No" that haven't quite stood the test of time.

Industry observers note that another sign of the zeitgeist in the 1962 film is that everyone smokes, which is a no-no by today's Hollywood standards. Cigarettes are found everywhere in the old film, from the casino to the hotel bar — and even the bedroom.

Smoking was commonplace in the US in the 1970s, so naturally this came across on the silver screen. In the 1970s TV series "Space: 1999" people were even depicted smoking on the moon, but by the 2000s, smoking was largely banned in many parts of the world due to its health risks.

One can also note in "Dr. No" that few people are wearing seat belts. When Bond drives off in his sports car to visit a woman, he is followed and a chase scene ensues. Bond, notably, is not wearing a seat belt.

According to recent reports, his pursuers eventually drive off a slope and die, of course — after all, they aren't wearing seat belts either and cars didn't have airbags at the time. The vehicle explodes, prompting 007 to say, "They were obviously in a hurry to get to their own funeral.".

In the older Bond films, all secretaries and receptionists are played by women, which in the 1960s, were considered standard female jobs.

Whether redheaded, blonde or brunette, secretaries are Bond's favorite targets for womanizing and they are all susceptible to his charms.

Throughout most Bond films, the agent has a romantic tension with Moneypenny, his boss's secretary, something which was not described in the original books.

Sources indicate that in the 2012 film "Skyfall" Moneypenny is given a first name: Eve, and we finally learn her backstory. In this film, she is no longer a hopeless secretary in love, but a top-trained agent who accidentally shoots Bond and is reassigned to desk duty as punishment.

In any case, today Moneypenny's job title today would probably be "Office Manager" or "Executive Assistant" rather than "Secretary.".

Sources indicate that in the film, Dr. No tells James Bond that he is the child of a British missionary and a Chinese woman from an upstanding family. However, the character is portrayed by Canadian actor Joseph Wiseman who is wearing makeup to make his eyes look more "Asian.".

While it used to be the norm in such movies to have East Asian characters played by white actors, today these cases of "yellowface" are frowned upon — just as it would be to wear blackface, putting black makeup on one's skin to portray a Black person.

Sources indicate that if there was a "Dr. No" remake in the future, a Chinese actor would be more likely to play this role.

Daniel Craig already paved the way in modernizing James Bond by stripping away campy gadgets, punchlines and invincibility, replacing them with a grounded, psychological and emotionally vulnerable portrayal of a post-9/11 spy.

According to recent reports, now it is up to Robert Pattinson to revisit the famous MI6 agent. Film critics believe his background will allow him to add dark sophistication and nonconformism to the iconic espionage role.

Throughout his career, Robert Pattinson has managed to combine roles in blockbuster hits and indie gems, from Bruce Wayne in "The Batman" to a disposable worker who is cloned every time he dies in "Mickey 17.".

Pattinson already has experience with classic spy archetypes: As the mysterious Neil in Christopher Nolan's sci-fi action thriller "Tenet," he assisted the protagonist in a time-bending espionage mission. He is also known for his eccentric personality and deadpan humor — qualities that could be useful for a modern Bond.

This article was translated from German by Sarah Hucal. It was first published in 2025 and updated following news of Robert Pattinson's casting as James Bond on November 16, 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, are you looking for a movie to thoroughly wallop you? To leave you emotionally battered, physically exhausted, and full of despair and hope at the same time? Then allow me to prescribe a healthy dose of The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping, the sixth film in the Hunger Games series.

Based on Suzanne Collins' second prequel novel following The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, Sunrise on the Reaping once again rewinds the clock on Panem to the 50th Hunger Games, otherwise known as the Second Quarter Quell. These are the biggest Hunger Games yet, with 48 tributes instead of the standard 24. Among them is Haymitch Abernathy (Joseph Zada), future mentor to series protagonists Katniss Everdeen and Peeta Mellark.

The question here is not whether Haymitch will survive the games. We know, by virtue of the entire original trilogy, that he does. But before he was the cynical, heavy-drinking, lone wolf victor audiences met in The Hunger Games, he was an optimistic 16-year-old with a caring family, a loving relationship, and a solid community in District 12. So the real question of Sunrise on the Reaping becomes, what broke that young man down so thoroughly? The answer is, unsurprisingly, bleak as all hell. But director Francis Lawrence executes it in thrilling (if occasionally overstuffed) fashion, with a Hunger Games sequence that blows series-high Catching Fire's own games out of the water, and a dogged focus on the philosophical themes at the core of Collins' work.

It has been revealed that this being a Hunger Games movie, there are certain key beats it needs to hit. First, tributes need to be reaped. In this case, District 12's motley crew is made up of Haymitch, Wyatt Callow (Ben Wang), Maysilee Donner (Mckenna Grace), and Louella McCoy (Molly McCann). From there, the tributes must go to the Capitol and witness its gaudy depravity for themselves. They get makeovers, train, give interviews, and eventually make their way into the Capitol's ultimate death trap.

Industry observers note that viewers have seen these beats before in The Hunger Games and Catching Fire. They also witnessed a deliberately scaled-back version in prequel The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes, which established the Games' evolution from what was essentially a run-down cage match to a glossy propaganda spectacle.

It has been revealed that after sending us through three very different Hunger Games, how can the franchise create a latest variation on the same brutal theme? First, by making Sunrise on the Reaping a heist movie. Granted, Haymitch and his allies aren't actually trying to steal anything from the Capitol. Rather, they're trying to break the arena and send a clear message. For that, Haymitch gets roped into a scheme cooked up by former victor Beetee (Kelvin Harrison Jr.) and his son, District 3 tribute Ampert (Percy Daggs IV). With a complex series of moving parts, Ampert and Haymitch's plan captures the essence of a dangerous heist, and Lawrence delivers the suspense to match.

Then, there's the arena. If you thought Catching Fire's clock was a sadistic marvel of game-making, not to mention a visual feast thanks to its tropical jungles and beaches, get ready for a level up. The arena for the Second Quarter Quell is a technicolor nightmare. Lush flower beds and crystal clear streams hide poisonous underbellies. Swarms of beautiful birds and butterflies will kill at a moment's notice. Even an idyllic, snow-capped mountain hides explosive horrors. Thankfully, Sunrise on the Reaping is actually colorful to match, its eye-popping hues reminding blockbuster filmmakers everywhere that yes, vibrancy is still possible!

Sources indicate that that vibrancy in Sunrise on the Reaping extends to the broader world of Panem itself, which has taken on a distinctive '70s look. The Capitol is awash in glitzy psychedelics, a far cry from the post-war dilapidation of The Ballad of Songbirds and Snakes. As the Games have grown more extravagant, so, too have the Capitol citizens. Take District 12 escort Drusilla Sickle (Glenn Close, almost unrecognizable under prosthetics and an uncanny tape facelift). She is the pinnacle of excess, from her visible cosmetic work to her neon fashion. Close is chewing so much scenery she could probably devour the entire arena, but it's exactly what the role calls for: ridiculous pomp, circumstance, and venomous hatred for the Districts.

Drusilla is one of the new characters introduced in Sunrise on the Reaping. However, a big chunk of the film's supporting cast is made up of familiar figures from the original trilogy: Capitol insider Plutarch Heavensbee (Jesse Plemons); master of ceremonies Caesar Flickerman (Kieran Culkin); former victors Beetee, Mags (Lili Taylor), and Wiress (Maya Hawke); stylist Effie Trinket (Elle Fanning); and of course, President Coriolanus Snow (Ralph Fiennes). Their non-stop introductions give Sunrise on the Reaping an unfortunate case of prequel-itis, even if they play key roles in the story. Their presence also means the involvement of many new Capitol characters feels muted. Billy Porter's snake-loving stylist Magno Stift gets short shrift (and even shorter screen time), while his helpers Proserpina (Iris Apatow) and Vitus (Edvin Ryding) might as well be afterthoughts.

Thankfully, the District 12 newcomers fare far better. As Haymitch's great love Lenore Dove, Whitney Peak is a radiant beam of rebellious wisdom. Elsewhere, each of the tributes buck misconceptions about them to reveal their true mettle underneath. Maysilee may seem stuck-up and aloof at first, but Grace quickly unleashes the ferocious survivor in her. Wang brings kind courage to oddsmaker Wyatt, and McCann is steely sweet as Louella.

Leading it all is Zada, who does an admirable job making Haymitch his own, all while balancing Harrelson's mannerisms from the original trilogy. Put them saying "sweetheart" side by side and tell me that's not the same character, years apart.

Sunrise on the Reaping works hard to build out this captivating latest version of Panem and the Games, but once it starts really playing in that sandbox, you're in for wave after wave of brutality. It's almost impressive how, after five books and six movies, the Hunger Games franchise can still find new ways to up the emotional pain of watching children fight to death under the thumb of an authoritarian regime. You'd think we'd already hit that peak with Rue's death in the first Hunger Games, and yet!

No spoilers, but let's just say I hope Zada's contract included a bonus for each time he had to cradle the body of a dear ally and tearfully beg them to stay with him. That his performance and the film never feel stale as they go through the motions of helpless grief time and time again is a testament to how distinct each of Haymitch's relationships feel.

Sources indicate that but while Sunrise on the Reaping is arguably the Hunger Games at its most tragic, it's also the franchise at its angriest. Every instalment in the series has critiqued the Capitol, but Sunrise on the Reaping puts a laser focus on the mundane machinery that keeps these systems of power in place. As the film opens, we see Peacekeepers and Capitol staffers performing administrative tasks for the Reaping, like putting up barricades and placards dictating where children should stand. Elsewhere, the propaganda machine chugs along, with cameramen like Plutarch always finding the perfect shot to tell the Capitol's story. (And always knowing which context to leave out to make the Capitol look its absolute best.).

In a recent development, throughout, though, Sunrise on the Reaping also turns its lens on Panem's citizens, asking why they allow themselves to be ruled by such a horrific regime. Collins opens Sunrise on the Reaping with several epigraphs, including two from Scottish philosopher David Hume, the first of which details his thoughts on implicit submission. The film takes that message to heart, repeatedly questioning what leads the many not to rise up against the few that govern them. Why do District 12's citizens stand mutely by while Drusilla and Plutarch re-stage a key moment from the Reaping ceremony? Why do armed tributes not turn on the unarmed Peacekeepers who oversee them at training? Sunrise on the Reaping doesn't take a subtle approach — at one point Plutarch straight-up says "no more implicit submission" — but then again, it's also vital to see a blockbuster not sand down the novel's overt messaging.

According to recent reports, it's also vital for a film this heavy to have hope, and almost miraculously, Sunrise on the Reaping, does. The film emphasizes the fact of its title: that for Haymitch's whole life, the sun has always risen on the Reaping. But as Lenore tells him, just because that's the way things have been for so long doesn't mean they'll be that way forever. (Their conversation remixes the novel's second epigraph from Hume.).

Sources indicate that anyone who's watched or read the original Hunger Games series knows that Panem will one day see a world where the sun doesn't rise on the Reaping. It'll just take a lot of work and sacrifice to get there. In Sunrise on the Reaping, we get to witness the first sparks of that eventual reunion. Knowing where Haymitch's story ends turns his tragedy into a bittersweet bridge to the future, making Sunrise on the Reaping a perfect bookend to the Hunger Games franchise as it stands. (At least, until Collins decides to return to Panem.).

The Hunger Games: Sunrise on the Reaping hits theaters Nov. 20.

Scientists discover a bizarre paradox among endangered penguins

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest study from the University of Otago, Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka, has revealed a surprising divide in the fortunes of one of New Zealand's least understood penguin species.
  • Published in PLOS ONE, the research found that one population has remained stable for at least 25 years, while the other has declined by more than 40 percent over the past three decades.
  • Recent findings suggest that the study was led by Dr.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest study from the University of Otago, Ōtākou Whakaihu Waka, has revealed a surprising divide in the fortunes of one of New Zealand's least understood penguin species. Although Erect-crested penguins breed in just two remote island groups, their populations are experiencing dramatically different outcomes.

Published in PLOS ONE, the research found that one population has remained stable for at least 25 years, while the other has declined by more than 40 percent over the past three decades.

Recent findings suggest that the study was led by Dr. Thomas Mattern of the Tawaki Project, which brings together scientists from the university's Departments of Zoology and Marine Science. Researchers also collaborated with the Antarctic Research Trust and the Global Penguin Society.

Drone Surveys Reveal a Surprising Penguin Population Divide.

Erect-crested penguins breed exclusively on the Bounty and Antipodes islands, two isolated island groups located approximately 800 kilometers southeast of Upcoming Zealand's South Island.

To determine how many penguins remain, researchers conducted extensive drone surveys between 2022 and 2024. They photographed and counted every breeding colony across both island groups, producing the first comprehensive population survey of the entire species.

Sources indicate that "The results overturn a long-standing assumption," Dr. Mattern says.

"The tiny Bounty Islands, at just 50 hectares, were found to hold almost as many breeding pairs (about 27,800) as the Antipodes Islands (about 29,800), even though the latter is 40 times larger and historically considered the species' stronghold.".

The difference in population trends was even more unexpected. Despite their small size, the Bounty Islands have maintained a relatively consistent number of breeding penguins for decades. Meanwhile, the much larger Antipodes Islands have experienced a substantial decline.

"Comparing the new counts with historical records going back to the mid-1990s, the Bounty Islands population has remained essentially unchanged for at least 25 years.

"The Antipodes Islands population, by contrast, has declined by more than 40 percent since 1995.".

Why Are Penguins Disappearing From the Antipodes Islands?

Researchers believe several overlapping pressures may explain why the two populations are heading in opposite directions. Natural predators, increasingly destructive storms, and differences in where the birds travel and feed could all be contributing.

It has been revealed that one particularly troubling factor involves skuas, native subantarctic birds that prey on penguin eggs and chicks. As penguin colonies become smaller, the birds lose some of the protection that comes from nesting together in large numbers.

"As Antipodes colonies have shrunk over recent decades, the collective defense they once provided against native subantarctic bird, the skua, a natural predator of eggs and chicks, has weakened, allowing predation losses to increase and colonies to fragment further.".

Co-author Dr. Klemens Pütz of the Antarctic Research Trust suggests that changes involving another penguin species may have intensified this pressure.

Industry observers note that eastern Rockhopper penguins suffered a "catastrophically" severe population collapse during the second half of the 20th century. Similar declines occurred across their Southern Ocean breeding range, likely driven by warming ocean waters. Today, fewer than 1,000 breeding pairs remain on the Antipodes Islands.

According to recent reports, "As Rockhoppers disappeared, skuas may have turned to Erect-crested penguin eggs and chicks instead," Dr. Pütz says.

Stronger Storms and Different Migration Routes Add to the Threat.

It has been revealed that predators are not the only challenge facing the Antipodes penguins. Increasingly powerful storms, consistent with wider climate trends across the Southern Ocean, have caused landslides that break up breeding colonies and leave the birds more vulnerable.

Differences in ocean habitats and seasonal movements may also help explain why the two populations have experienced such contrasting outcomes.

Recent findings suggest that according to Dr. Mattern, penguins breeding on the Antipodes Islands migrate considerable distances into the Antarctic Polar Frontal Zone when the breeding season ends. In contrast, birds from the Bounty Islands remain closer to their nesting grounds, where the surrounding waters are more sheltered and may offer more abundant food.

These differences could leave the two populations exposed to very different environmental pressures, despite belonging to the same species.

The Strange Paradox of Schrödinger's Penguin.

The researchers have named this unusual situation "Schrödinger's Penguin," drawing inspiration from the famous physics thought experiment involving a cat inside a sealed box.

In that experiment, the cat is imagined to be both alive and dead until the box is opened and its condition is observed. But Dr. Mattern explains that the penguin discovery turns the familiar concept around.

"With Schrödinger's cat, opening the box settles the question one way or the other.

Recent findings suggest that "With Erect-crested penguins, it's the opposite. From a distance, without proper surveys, everyone assumed there was a single answer for the whole species.

"Once we actually opened the metaphorical box and looked, we found there wasn't one state at all, but two: stable on the Bounty Islands, declining on the Antipodes Islands.".

It has been revealed that in other words, looking at the species as a whole can conceal what is happening within individual populations. Only by examining both island groups separately did researchers uncover how dramatically their circumstances differ.

A Hidden Conservation Crisis for Endangered Penguins.

Industry observers note that the Erect-crested penguin is currently one of only four penguin species worldwide classified as "Endangered" on the International Union for Conservation of Nature Red List. Another New Zealand penguin, the hoiho/yellow-eyed penguin, shares that designation.

Sources indicate that however, the two species have received very different levels of attention. While the plight of the hoiho has attracted ongoing public interest and conservation efforts, the Erect-crested penguin has remained relatively overlooked.

Industry observers note that dr. Mattern explains that the species' current conservation classification relies on population estimates from the 1970s that were considerably inflated. When the new survey results are considered, the "Endangered" designation remains broadly appropriate for the declining Antipodes population, but not for the stable Bounty Islands population.

This creates a difficult conservation dilemma. If the two populations are combined into a single assessment, the species' overall threat classification could actually improve, even though one population continues to decline sharply.

"Averaged across both populations, the global ranking would actually improve to "Vulnerable," masking the severity of the Antipodes decline, and downplaying how exposed the Bounty Islands, likely the species' last secure stronghold, are to industrial fishing.".

In a recent development, the researchers warn that a more favorable overall classification could create a misleading impression of security. Although the Bounty Islands population remains stable, it may still face significant threats, particularly from industrial fishing activity.

According to recent reports, "A single, ostensibly improved threat ranking is like putting the lid back on Schrödinger's box, trading a convenient illusion for the stronger protection the Bounty Islands population actually needs," Dr. Mattern notes.

The findings highlight why conservation efforts must account for the circumstances of individual populations rather than relying exclusively on a species' global status. For Erect-crested penguins, recognizing the differences between the two island groups could be essential to protecting their future.

The study received funding from the Vontobel Foundation (Switzerland) through the Antarctic Research Trust and from the Global Penguin Society. The research was carried out under permits issued by the Newly introduced Zealand Department of Conservation.

Materials provided by University of Otago. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sixteen-year-old Summer McIntosh broke the world record for the 400m individual medley at the Canadian swimming trials on Saturday – just days after breaking the world record for the 400m freestyle.

McIntosh finished the 400m individual medley in a time of 4:25.87, breaking the mark set at the 2016 Rio Olympics by Hungarian swimmer Katinka Hosszú with a time of 4:26.36.

The result continues the teenager’s brilliant week after she broke the 400m freestyle world record last Tuesday – breaking defending Olympic champion Ariarne Titmus’ previous record of 3:56.40, which was set last May, in a time of 3:56.08.

Speaking after her latest triumph, McIntosh shared her emotions.

“That’s the first time I really vividly heard the crowd during my race,” McIntosh noted, per Reuters.

“It’s amazing to have all my family and friends in the stands, cheering me on. It really helped me in the last 100 meters.”.

The Canadian teen made her Olympic debut aged 14 at Tokyo 2020, where she finished fourth in the 200-meter freestyle.

She bagged gold in the 200m butterfly and 400m medley at the world championships in 2022, as well as two golds at the Commonwealth Games in the 200m and 400m medleys.

She now trains in Florida under coach Brent Arckey with the Sarasota Sharks team.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ben White has made eight appearances for England.

Ben White's crucial goal against world champions Spain on Sunday will not be forgotten by England fans for a long time.

According to recent reports, A smart finish to cap a flowing Three Lions move gave Thomas Tuchel's men an almost unbelievable 3-0 lead in Madrid. They hung on - just - meaning White will always be remembered as the player who scored that winner.

But, for White, the moment represented more than just a goal. It signalled a dramatic turnaround in fortunes for his international career - just four years after many thought his England days were over.

The Arsenal defender has had a tough time on the international stage to say the least.

He left the World Cup in 2022 after a disagreement with then assistant manager Steve Holland and made himself unavailable during the rest of Gareth Southgate's time in charge.

Since returning to England duty in March under Tuchel, the 29-year-old has now established himself as arguably England's best right-back - despite facing jeers from sections of his own fans for his decision to leave that camp.

The defender, who initially arrived at Arsenal from Brighton as a centre-back, has had an excellent start to the season, having played a crucial part in the Gunners' first title win for 22 years last time out.

It hasn't been straightforward for him at Arsenal either though. White has had to navigate his own injury problems and at one point when the defender was struggling for fitness, there was talk that the Gunners should look at moving him on.

But White has battled back and even dealt with competition from Jurrien Timber to remain one of Arsenal's key players.

People don't know full story behind England exile - White.

60 minutes of perfection, 30 minutes of chaos - an England win for the ages.

"I think just obviously people don't know the full story, because I never said anything and won't put anyone under the bus", White said before the England win over Spain.

The 29-year-old is keen to put the well-covered departure from the World Cup in Qatar behind him.

After his long absence from playing for England, some supporters did not believe that White should return.

His first appearance at Wembley since that incident in a friendly against Uruguay in March was booed by some supporters, loud enough for Tuchel to be asked about it after the match.

That game in itself was dramatic for White, who scored the opening goal for England before giving away the penalty that saw the Three Lions draw 1-1 with Uruguay.

White, who missed the World Cup with injury, had been expecting the reaction from some fans. But he is used to proving himself and changing the perception around him.

Tuchel was keen to back his player and said in the build-up to the Spain game that he hoped that the chapter was closed on White being booed by his own supporters.

"Obviously a bit tricky and not straightforward, but yes, it's obviously amazing to be here now." White noted of his return to England.

White said in that same interview that he would make the same decision again that he did at the World Cup, but it was now time to move on.

His displays show exactly where his mindset is for his country.

He played the final 12 minutes in England's win over Croatia at Wembley before being brought into the starting line-up for England's toughest match of the November international break against Spain.

This new era of England is being dubbed Tuchel 2.0 and White firmly seems to be part of it.

Sources indicate that chelsea defender Reece James is out with injury. He is a big favourite of Tuchel's but cannot be relied upon for every game due to injuries.

According to recent reports, white is a key player for the Premier League champions, reliable in defence and a threat in attack while being physically imposing. There is a lot for Tuchel to like.

And with three of his Arsenal team-mates on the pitch as England won the game, and Bukayo Saka to return, White brings the positives of the cohesion of a club side to Tuchel's team.

Arsenal supporters will not be surprised by White's excellent performances for England.

Since signing for the Gunners in 2021, not many players can say they have played more of a crucial role in Arsenal's rebirth under Mikel Arteta.

Such is the importance of White, the Gunners attack does not flow as freely when he is not in the side to link up with Martin Odegaard and Saka as he relentlessly produces overlapping runs - a trait he demonstrated when he scored England's third in Madrid.

His team-mates regularly say he is one of the fiercest competitors in training, and he has regularly shown his mentality when it looks as though things are going against him with his club side.

Arsenal signing Timber and a number of injury complications looked to have had White nearing an exit but, such is his determination, each time a challenge comes up he manages to turn it around.

White is a unique character within football, and has even said he doesn't watch the game away from the training ground, but his passion for his profession cannot be doubted.

Gunners fans will know that the level of passion he displayed in Madrid is something he shows every time he is on the pitch for his club side.

Latest Update: Fiona the Hippo Died After Eating a Hat. But How Does a Hat Kill a Hippo?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1629 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s famous hippo who charmed observers around the world, tragically died on Thursday due to medical complications after ingesting a knit hat that mistakenly entered her enclosure last week, according to zoo officials.
  • In a recent development, according to zoo officials, the hat that caused her death entered her enclosure after a child tossed it into the air.
  • Recent findings suggest that for nonexperts, Fiona’s tragic death raises several questions: Why and how would a knit hat kill a hippo that weighs more than 2,500 pounds?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that fiona, the Cincinnati Zoo’s famous hippo who charmed observers around the world, tragically died on Thursday due to medical complications after ingesting a knit hat that mistakenly entered her enclosure last week, according to zoo officials. Fiona was just nine years old when she died.

In a recent development, according to zoo officials, the hat that caused her death entered her enclosure after a child tossed it into the air. The hat reportedly collided with a ceiling fan, which then released the hat through a “one-foot gap above the 12-foot-tall viewing window.” A few days after eating the hat, her condition began to deteriorate.

Recent findings suggest that for nonexperts, Fiona’s tragic death raises several questions: Why and how would a knit hat kill a hippo that weighs more than 2,500 pounds? Why wasn’t surgery possible for Fiona? And, for zookeepers, what was the range of treatment scenarios available?

Jan Hawkins, the head of the clinical science department at North Carolina State University’s College of Veterinary Medicine, tells WIRED that—with the caveat that we won’t officially know until doctors conduct a post-mortem analysis—Fiona’s death was likely due to one of a few downstream effects of the hat getting caught somewhere in her intestinal tract.

In a sense, an intestinal blockage in a hippo is like a car crash on an incredibly long one-lane highway. Hawkins stated that, estimating, a hippo’s intestinal tract is likely over 100 feet long, with more than 70 feet in the small intestines alone. In humans, the lengths of the small and large intestines are a comparably diminutive 25 feet.

Sources indicate that hawkins says that in a healthy hippo, liquids can take as little as 12 hours to pass, and food takes two to three days. According to zoo officials, Fiona ate the hat on or about Sunday, November 8. Zoo officials claimed that Fiona was asymptomatic at first but began to lose her appetite after a few days. If the hat was going to come out, Hawkins says it likely would have happened within five days. So what happened?

In a recent development, one possibility, Hawkins claims, is that when the hat got stuck, it caused a huge amount of swelling and pressure in her abdomen. That swelling could have led to her blood circulation being cut off and, eventually, to tissue death. After becoming green or black, Hawkins says, dead tissue is more likely to leak, and perhaps rupture, releasing the contents of the digestive tract into her blood. This can easily cause toxic shock.

It has been revealed that in Fiona’s situation, this would mean that bacteria in her digestive tract died and released toxic molecules. If these toxins enter the bloodstream, Hawkins says, that would cause the organs to become more and more inflamed. Ultimately, this can lead to organ failure and death.

Another possibility is that, after the hat got stuck, Fiona’s intestines began to “twist on itself,” Hawkins notes. This would be more likely if the hat, say, got pieces of food stuck inside of it, gradually becoming larger and heavier. Intestines are supposed to contract and move as they digest food. This means that if a heavy object gets stuck, the intestine can start to twist around it. In severe cases, this can cut off blood circulation. Eventually, this too can lead to tissue death. This initiates the chain of intestines leaking or rupturing, toxins entering the bloodstream, and organs becoming inflamed and eventually failing.

According to recent reports, we don’t know exactly where the hat was in Fiona’s digestive tract. In a video the Cincinnati Zoo published to X on Tuesday, however, an unnamed staffer claimed that an ultrasound indicated “some bunching of intestines.” They believed this meant that Fiona was “passing some things through her small intestine.”.

If the hat was in Fiona’s small intestine, this would have meant that it passed through all three of her stomachs. (Hippos have three stomachs.) This could provide some hints about the type of hat that Fiona ate.

According to recent reports, hawkins says that in hippos, all three of their stomachs have the same basic components, but in different amounts. The first stomach has the largest amount of bacteria and protozoa, which help break down significant pieces of food in the earliest part of digestion. The third has the highest amounts of enzymes and hydrochloric acid, which reduce food scraps into their smallest possible size before entering the small intestine.

In a recent development, “Let’s say it was a cotton hat or some sort of organic material, it’s possible that that could partially break down,” Hawkins tells WIRED. “Whereas if it had something that would not degrade—so a plastic, or polyester, or something like that—then obviously its character is not gonna break down at all.”.

The effects of this, Hawkins claims, would be even more severe if the hat were rigid or not collapsible in any way. “If it wouldn’t get scrunched down, like a hair scrunchie, then you could understand why it would get stuck,” Hawkins says. “Because it can’t change its character as much.”.

All of this, Hawkins indicates, may have affected whether Fiona was able to pass the hat.

Recent findings suggest that according to the Cincinnati Zoo’s Tuesday video, conducting surgery to remove the hat would not be possible for Fiona. The zoo said that a combination of specialists—including “veterinarian human specialists,” zoo employees, and “other experts”—came to the conclusion that surgery wasn’t the best option and that the “best chance for success with Fiona would be if she can pass this on her own.”.

Rebecca Lewison, a San Diego State University biology professor and cochair of the Hippo Specialist Group of the International Union for Conservation of Nature, tells WIRED that when it comes to hippo surgery, a major challenge is their “unpredictable and irregular responses to sedation and anesthesia.”.

“It is very risky for [hippos], and they can die from the standard medication used on other large animals, like elephants and rhinos, for reasons we don’t well understand,” Lewison tells WIRED.

It has been revealed that there are also some inherent challenges to administering anesthesia to an animal as large as Fiona. When a human or animal goes under anesthesia, they need to be put on a ventilator that artificially breathes for them. An animal that weighs more than 2,500 pounds, Hawkins claims, requires a ventilator of a much different scale than what humans need for general surgery.

Sources indicate that fiona was placed under anesthesia to conduct bloodwork, according to the Cincinnati Zoo’s Tuesday video. But Hawkins claims that the amount of anesthesia required for bloodwork is much smaller than what would be required for a major surgery, like removing a foreign object from her intestines. For Fiona, the increased amount of anesthesia alone increases the risk of the surgery.

Another fact to consider, Hawkins says, is the position the zoo would feasibly be able to place her in while conducting surgery. If a human is in surgery, they may be placed on their back, on their stomach, on their side, or in a variety of other positions. With animals like hippos, Hawkins says, this gets more complicated.

“You would have to have a hoist, a forklift or something, to pick them up to put them on either a pad or on a table,” Hawkins says. And if a zoo doesn’t have a table that’s big enough, the animal may have to go on the floor.

Sources indicate that but Hawkins notes that even at perfectly resourced zoos, there are other risks for hippos. In order to perform a major surgery, an animal as large as Fiona would have to have a huge amount of anesthesia, putting her unconscious and in the same position for a long period of time. She would have her entire body weight putting pressure on the parts of her body that can’t move. This would limit her body’s ability to circulate oxygen—even with the help of a great ventilator.

Industry observers note that if an animal is unhealthy, Hawkins indicates, the risks are even greater. In its Tuesday video, the Cincinnati Zoo stated that when it recently ran some tests on Fiona, it found that she was dehydrated. This means that her body was already working extra hard to circulate blood not only to the blockage but also through the rest of her body.

Animal caretakers in this position, Hawkins indicates, face incredibly difficult choices.

With surgery ruled out, the Cincinnati Zoo claims to have used a variety of other methods to help Fiona. In the Tuesday video, the zoo claimed that her early bloodwork did not raise any red flags. Zookeepers then conducted an ultrasound and administered rectal fluids, an enema, and medication, including some to help with vomiting and nausea. Later, the Tuesday video claims, the zoo “borrowed a nine-foot scope from Columbus Zoo” with the goal of getting “far enough up to reach something.”.

On Wednesday, Cincinnati Zoo said in a post that it had borrowed a “vibration plate” from a local horse farm with the hope that it would “encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass.”.

The zoo remarked that it also encouraged Fiona to eat and offered her some of her favorite foods.

“Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she always has really liked, and they were happy to see her respond,” the zoo said Wednesday evening.

It has been revealed that but in the end, it wasn’t enough, but not for lack of trying. Hawkins notes it sounds like “they threw everything at her but the kitchen sink.”.

Hawkins adds, “I think they did not want to leave a stone unturned.”.

Breaking: Feds arrest top official of healthcare company, alleging illegal drug importation

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • authorities are accusing the two top officials of a Canadian manufacturer of operating a long-running scheme to illegally import prescription drugs into the U.S., according to court records filed Tuesday.
  • John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of the organization, CANARX, was arrested Sunday on smuggling and conspiracy charges, according to the records.
  • Bob Howard, his brother, who is president and a director of CANARX, is also wanted in the federal investigation, according to an affidavit from Dustin Dobbs, a special agent with the Food and Drug Administration's Office of Criminal Investigations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that U.S. authorities are accusing the two top officials of a Canadian manufacturer of operating a long-running scheme to illegally import prescription drugs into the U.S., according to court records filed Tuesday.

John Thomas Howard, treasurer and a director of the organization, CANARX, was arrested Sunday on smuggling and conspiracy charges, according to the records.

Bob Howard, his brother, who is president and a director of CANARX, is also wanted in the federal investigation, according to an affidavit from Dustin Dobbs, a special agent with the Food and Drug Administration's Office of Criminal Investigations. He has not yet been taken into custody.

Besides conspiracy and smuggling, the arrest warrant said John Thomas Howard was charged with introducing misbranded drugs into interstate commerce and illegal drug importation. No plea has been filed.

According to recent reports, CANARX was featured in a CNBC investigation last year that revealed how the tech giant and others known as alternative funding programs, or AFPs, are becoming more pervasive around the U.S. as drug costs skyrocket. The investigation found these companies have penetrated the country's healthcare system by offering high-cost specialty drugs at more affordable prices through private and public employers. In some cases, employers are requiring their staff to use an AFP.

Recent findings suggest that AFPs often obtain the medications overseas and ship them directly to patients, a practice that federal authorities have said is illegal and poses safety risks. CNBC traced the trail of drugs from abroad to the U.S. via a supply chain that the pharmaceutical companies producing the medications have not authorized.

Recent findings suggest that on its website, CANARX, founded in 2002 and based in Windsor, Ontario, Canada, described its business as the first international prescription provider for the U.S. and the safest such program in the industry. The firm noted it sources its medications from Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia and New Zealand.

But the affidavit stated that the FDA's investigation found "there is probable cause to believe that (CANARX) illegally imported or caused the illegal importation of prescription drugs into the United States ….".

Industry observers note that the affidavit does not specify which medications the agency believes were illegally imported. The criminal complaint covers the period from Feb. 22, 2017, through April 15, 2026.

The company's general counsel, Joseph Morris, told CNBC in a statement: "The Howards deny all the charges against them, will defend vigorously, and expect to be vindicated in court.".

Sources indicate that the organization has been under FDA scrutiny for several years. In 2023, the agency seized medication being shipped by CANARX that it says was potentially misbranded and counterfeit, according to an email sent to a patient that was obtained by CNBC.

And in 2019, the FDA sent a warning letter to the manufacturer, saying it was operating "in a manner that substitutes the FDA-approved drugs prescribed by the U.S. healthcare provider with unapproved drugs." Morris, in response to that warning, argued CANARX was not misleading patients, but agreed for the company to stop importing drugs that need to be administered by a doctor.

According to recent reports, in an interview as part of the CNBC investigation, Morris said last year that the medicines shipped to U.S. patients come from highly regulated countries. He said CANARX was operating legally.

Sources indicate that the central question for AFPs is the legality of importing prescription drugs into the U.S. for personal use. The FDA allows Americans to import medications for individual use in some cases if the drug is not available domestically. That is the basis on which the AFPs built their models for shipping medicines directly to patients.

According to recent reports, but an FDA spokesperson told CNBC last year that "in most circumstances, a person cannot import prescription drugs from other countries into the U.S. ... as substitutes for FDA-approved drugs.".

In a separate civil lawsuit that is pending, Gilead Sciences accused CANARX and other companies of illegally importing Biktarvy, its medication to treat HIV.

Industry observers note that in a statement to CNBC on Wednesday, a Gilead spokesperson mentioned the company "has taken strong legal action to protect patients and the integrity of the U.S. medicines supply chain. We welcome the government's efforts to hold accountable those whose conduct may put patients at risk.".

CANARX has not responded to the Gilead lawsuit.

— CNBC's Paige Tortorelli and Melissa Lee contributed to this report.

Physicists use laser light to unlock a crystal's hidden electrical powers

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (899 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Physicists at Auburn University have discovered how to use brief bursts of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions hidden inside a crystal.
  • Sources indicate that the research was led by Wencan Jin, the Thomas and Jean Walter Endowed Associate Professor in Auburn's Department of Physics, and graduate student Mohamed Kandil.
  • The researchers investigated a modified version of strontium titanate, a material with an unusual combination of electrical characteristics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Physicists at Auburn University have discovered how to use brief bursts of laser light to organize tiny electrical regions hidden inside a crystal. Their findings shed new light on a mystery that has puzzled researchers for decades and demonstrate how lasers can influence the material's electrical behavior. The breakthrough could eventually help scientists explore faster ways to process and store information.

Sources indicate that the research was led by Wencan Jin, the Thomas and Jean Walter Endowed Associate Professor in Auburn's Department of Physics, and graduate student Mohamed Kandil. Their paper, "Optical Poling of a Quantum Ferroelectric Metal across the Order-Disorder Phase Transition," received an Editors' Suggestion designation from Physical Review Letters. Scientists at Japan's National Institute of Advanced Industrial Science and Technology produced the crystals used in the study.

A Decades-Old Mystery Hidden Inside a Crystal.

The researchers investigated a modified version of strontium titanate, a material with an unusual combination of electrical characteristics. Although electrons can travel through the crystal, it also contains extremely small regions with positive and negative electrical sides. Known as polar nanoregions, these microscopic "islands" can point in different directions or become aligned with one another. Understanding how and why this alignment occurs is essential to explaining the material's properties and learning how to manipulate them.

In a recent development, scientists have spent decades trying to determine what happens when these regions become organized. One possibility is that atoms move together to produce the polarized state. Another is that the tiny electrical islands are already there and simply begin pointing in the same direction as temperatures fall. The distinction is similar to the difference between assembling a group of people and asking people who are already gathered to turn and face the same way. Because the regions are extraordinarily small and produce very weak signals, determining which explanation is correct has been a persistent challenge.

Laser Experiments Reveal How Electrical Order Emerges.

Sources indicate that to investigate, the Auburn researchers developed an exceptionally sensitive system that uses lasers to measure subtle changes in the crystal. By studying how the material altered incoming light, they were able to monitor the orientation of its electrical regions while repeatedly heating and cooling the sample.

The measurements revealed a clear pattern. At warmer temperatures, the tiny regions pointed in seemingly random directions. When the crystal cooled, however, they began adopting preferred orientations. This behavior provided compelling evidence that the electrical islands existed before becoming aligned, supporting the explanation that cooling organizes regions already present in the material.

A Flash of Light Creates Order in a Trillionth of a Second.

Industry observers note that the team went beyond observing this natural process. Researchers also demonstrated that short laser pulses could temporarily align the electrical islands, even at higher temperatures when the regions would ordinarily remain disorganized. Using an optical measurement, they were able to detect the pattern produced by the laser light.

The effect was extraordinarily brief, lasting approximately one picosecond, or one trillionth of a second. Nevertheless, the ability to create and detect this electrical alignment using light provides a promising approach for studying how information might be controlled at extremely high speeds.

Three Years of Experiments Lead to a Breakthrough.

Achieving these results required considerable patience and technical refinement. The collaboration began at the 2023 American Physical Society March Meeting, where Jin met Japanese researchers capable of producing the specialized crystals needed for the experiments.

According to recent reports, back at Auburn, the team spent almost a year refining its equipment before it could reliably detect the weak optical signals from the tiny electrical regions. The next obstacle was even more demanding: measuring the extremely short interval during which laser illumination caused the regions to align.

"The breakthrough came in 2025, when Mohamed finally observed the disordered polar regions becoming aligned under laser illumination," Jin mentioned. "Seeing that signal emerge was a thrilling moment for the team.".

The achievement also represents an key personal milestone for Kandil, whose first published research paper reflects three years of dedicated experimental work.

According to recent reports, "This experiment has truly been Mohamed's odyssey," Jin said. "It took him three years of dedication to complete the work and achieve his first publication.".

Fresh Possibilities for Ultrafast Information Technology.

Recent findings suggest that the discovery provides important evidence about how electrical order develops in this unusual crystal while also establishing a method for manipulating that order with light. Rather than simply observing the material's internal behavior, researchers can now briefly influence its microscopic electrical patterns and detect the resulting changes.

Industry observers note that although practical applications remain a future possibility, the experiments offer a latest way to investigate the rapid electrical processes occurring inside quantum materials. By revealing how light can control these previously elusive patterns, the Auburn researchers have opened another avenue for exploring technologies that could one day transform how information is processed and stored.

#47809. Should I buy a gaming console just to play GTA 6? That depends on your FOMO.

Should I buy a gaming console just to play GTA 6? That depends on your FOMO.

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1312 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mashable

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Grand Theft Auto VI is out now, if you hadn't heard.
  • Recent findings suggest that by that, we mean you might not have a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series console at the ready to play the highly anticipated release.
  • So, let's lay out the cases for and against doing that.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Grand Theft Auto VI is out now, if you hadn't heard. If you're not playing it but are reading this, we can guess why.

Recent findings suggest that by that, we mean you might not have a PlayStation 5 or Xbox Series console at the ready to play the highly anticipated release. If that's the case, you're going to miss out on the biggest gaming launch of the year — and possibly all time. FOMO is a natural human reaction to these sorts of things, and here at Mashable, we fully understand the pain of not being sure whether or not you should buy a console just for GTA 6.

So, let's lay out the cases for and against doing that.

The primary and most obvious reason to buy a console for GTA 6 is that it's the only real way to play it at launch. There is technically another way that we'll cover in a little while, but for all intents and purposes, you cannot have the same experience everyone else is having without buying a PS5 or Xbox Series console.

By all accounts, GTA 6 is a pretty fantastic video game. You probably wouldn't want to miss out on that. What are you going to do while everyone else is having an amazing time parading through Leonida, read books? Come on, that sounds boring.

Sources indicate that one thing that's also worth remembering is that other video games exist. A lot of them, in fact. If you buy a PS5 or Xbox Series console, you'll have access to the last six years of current-gen releases, some of which are extremely good. They might even be better than GTA 6! As a fun bonus, through the magic of backward compatibility, ports, remasters, and remakes, you'll also be able to play countless video games from previous generations of hardware, too.

In a recent development, lastly, both consoles (at least the models with disc drives) work as 4K Blu-ray players, if you're into collecting physical versions of movies. That's cool, too.

Both consoles have been hard to find in stock (thanks in large part to GTA 6), but the Xbox Series S and PS5 Digital Edition are both in stock at Amazon, as of this writing. If you're not sure whether to buy a PS5 or the Xbox Series X/S, keep scrolling for a breakdown of the pros and cons.

First, foremost, in the biggest, boldest font you can imagine: You shouldn't buy a console just for GTA 6 because they're stupid expensive these days.

In a recent development, both Xbox and PlayStation have recently increased the prices of their consoles due to real-world economic concerns. The cheapest model right now is a $499 Xbox Series S, and Rockstar hasn't shown us that version of the game yet, leading to speculation that the game is better on PS5, which starts at $599. If you want the best possible version at launch, you'll need a PS5 Pro, which costs $899 — and is presently out of stock at most retailers.

In other words, there just isn't a particularly affordable way to play GTA 6 traditionally at launch, unless you already own the hardware.

Recent findings suggest that there are, of course, other reasons to not get a console for GTA 6. There exists a slim likelihood that you won't like the game, though so far, most people who have played it have come away with positive impressions. It also won't have an online component at launch, and no one knows when it will get one. For a lot of people, GTA Online is the only GTA experience that matters, and that audience will have very little to do in the new game until some nebulous point in the future when Rockstar decides to cater to them.

It has been revealed that maybe you just don't care that much about non-GTA video games, either. If that's the case, it's hard to recommend spending this much money on a box that will only play one game.

There was a lot of anxiety on the internet prior to the game's launch surrounding the potential differences between the different console versions. The good news is that the game is out and has been fully tested by experts, and the verdict is that you almost can't go wrong with GTA 6 on any platform.

Digital Foundry is an outlet and YouTube channel that offers expert-level tech analysis of games, and they have a fairly comprehensive guide to the different console versions of GTA 6. According to DF, both the PS5 and Series X versions run at the same resolution and target the same frame rate, with some performance dips on both in more intense sequences. In other words, the base PS5 and Series X versions are roughly the same, though the PS5's controller does have exclusive haptic feedback features for gameplay like driving cars.

Industry observers note that there is also the matter of the PS5 Pro and Xbox Series S consoles, though. DF says the PS5 Pro is the best version of the game, with a sharper resolution and higher-quality shadows to go along with smoother performance. That was to be expected. Sadly, it sounds like the Series S version is probably the least desirable build of the game. Its visuals have been marginally downgraded with a lower resolution and some reduced visual settings, but more importantly, DF's analysis found that the frame rate can dip below 20fps in extreme circumstances.

We do have good news for Xbox Series S gamers, however. Mashable Editorial Director Eric Miller has played the game on Series S and has had a positive first impression so far. If you have no other way to play GTA 6, it should work, but it will be reduced in quality compared to the others.

There is technically a way to play GTA 6 without buying a newly introduced PS5 or Xbox, but it's not a viable alternative for most people.

Recent findings suggest that to be clear, there are multiple massive reasons why you might not want to do this. For starters, it involves a monthly subscription. Beyond that, Microsoft recently imposed strict monthly hour limits on Cloud Gaming. With this system, you will be able to play at most 15 hours of GTA 6 per month. Many people are going to play more than that in the first weekend it's out. Even if those aren't concerns, game streaming is subject to the limits of your home internet, meaning that latency and buffering can and will occur. That version of the game will also be visually downgraded to some degree, per Rockstar.

If game streaming (understandably) doesn't work for you, the last option is to wait for the PC version. Unfortunately, Rockstar has not said anything about when GTA 6 will launch on PC, though a recent report pegged it as coming in early 2027. That will likely be the best version of the game in terms of visuals, but only if you have the requisite hardware. For those who already have capable gaming PCs, this might be the best option for playing GTA 6, provided you're patient enough to wait. For those who don't, this is going to be even more expensive than buying a console, so maybe don't bother.

HBO Max — top pick for premium content.

Disney+ — best for families.

Peacock — low-cost choice for live sport.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voyager 1 has reached a historic milestone in space — it now takes a light-day to send a command to the spacecraft, meaning a full 24 hours for Earth to hail the distant spacecraft.

Since Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, released on an initial tour through the outer solar system in 1977, their missions have been packed with science. Voyager 1 looked at Jupiter and Saturn from up close before veering for a flyby of Saturn's moon Titan and Saturn's rings, a pathway that brought it above the plane of the solar system in the early 1980s.

Voyager 1's faster path out of the solar system brought it to one light-day in distance on Wednesday (Nov. 18), while Voyager 2 — which took a slightly slower track to see Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune — will reach a light-day of distance in 2035. So what's next for the two Voyager spacecraft as they reach further into interstellar space?

Interstellar space, which is the area where the sun's constant stream of solar particles within the heliopause gives way to the physics of interstellar space, has been a valuable harvest for both Voyagers. Voyager 1 crossed interstellar space in August 2012 and continues to get data, while Voyager 2 has done the same since November 2018.

According to recent reports, "Current science is continuing our investigation on magnetic field strength and direction, plasma density, and energetic particle detection. What is important is to measure how these phenomena change as the spacecraft travels further away from the sun," Suzanne Dodd, project manager for the Voyager missions at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), told Space.com in an email.

Added to that will be the Voyagers' examinations of plasma and magnetic fields nearby the spacecraft, and a focus on any "solar effects" such as shocks or pressure fronts, added JPL project scientist Linda Spilker in an email.

"Key Voyager science going forward includes observing the extent to which our sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1," Spilker continued. "Where does the sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may last long enough to answer that question.".

Sources indicate that the team also wants to watch the magnetic field around the spacecraft continue to change direction from the sun, to interstellar space, Spilker noted. That finding was not expected when the Voyagers released, so scientists are curious to know more — as long as the spacecraft can last, that is.

In a recent development, each Voyager continues to lose 4 watts of power a year; their launch power was 470 watts in 1977, and the nuclear power source continues to dwindle, requiring harder choices as the missions approach their 50th years of operations. Instruments have had to be shut off, and both the spacecraft were directed to perform a "Massive Bang" of power redistribution earlier this year to preserve as much power as possible without sacrificing science.

Looking forward, Dodd says the team does not anticipate having to make any major changes to spacecraft operations until after the 50th anniversary passes for each spacecraft next August and September (as Voyager 2 launched a few weeks before Voyager 1).

A JPL representative added that the "Big Bang" should keep the remaining science instruments going until that point, although "there is also the thermal state of the spacecraft to balance." The representative added that the margins for power remain "very thin," especially as the spacecraft are quite cold in interstellar space.

"Then there are the things the team can't predict, such as the unexpected loss of contact that happened recently," the spokesperson added, referring to an approximately 48-hour glitch in which Voyager 1 suddenly stopped responding to commands last month — although the spacecraft did promptly recover.

"The goal of the mission is science, so the team is not just concerned with keeping in contact with the Voyagers, but keeping the science instruments going as long as possible," the representative added. "The further away the spacecraft get from Earth, the more they learn about how interstellar space changes further away from the heliopause.".

Sources indicate that voyager 1 team members now represent multiple generations of engineers, each one of them with distinct but essential roles. Even the most junior members of the team—Nshan Kazaryan and Bhavana Gupta—are taking on key roles in anticipation of more responsibility in the future, according to JPL mission manager Kareem Badaruddin.

It has been revealed that "They have demonstrated their value to the team consistently," Badaruddin said in an email. Kazaryan's responsibilities include negotiating tracking schedules with the Deep Space Network (DSN), a set of three antennas for following distant missions, to keep tabs on the Voyagers. Gupta, meanwhile, has provided documentation to gather crucial details from the Voyagers' command and control systems to "give detailed instructions" in case of issues.

Recent findings suggest that "One of our most senior team members, Jack Lippincott, has provided critical knowledge and understanding of DSN operations and data interpretation," Badaruddin added. Pointing to one of the DSN antennas in Goldstone, California, he remarked the weather in that region "has been violent the last few weeks, and he has helped us to understand how to deal with unique problems that arose because of it.".

While there's no real sense of how much further the spacecraft could keep going, the team notes it's committed to be there as long as possible. "It has taken decades of exceptional engineering to get Voyager 1 to the one light-day milestone, and hopefully much further before the mission ends," Dodd said.

Badaruddin added: "One of the reasons that one light-day is so special is that it has never happened before that we were in contact with a spacecraft at this distance, and it may never happen again.".

Editor's note: This article was updated at 9 a.m. EST, Nov. 20, to correct the location of one of the DSN facilities to Goldstone, California (not Australia).

#47804. Dinosaurs may have been eating seaweed 100 million years ago
